bp: The paper is about a public knowledge store such as Wikipedia, PubMed, or a programming archive, where people both add material and learn from what is already there. Large language models now enter that loop in two ways: they can add text or code to the archive, and people can use them as helpers instead of studying the archive directly. That changes the web from a mostly human-built library into a shared human-machine system. The practical question is not simply whether machines can produce more content. It is whether the whole system keeps producing useful knowledge over time. The paper builds a small dynamical model, meaning a model that follows quantities as they change together: archive size, archive quality, model skill, human skill, and query volume. The goal is to see when growth is healthy, when machine output crowds out human contribution, and when quality or skill can decline despite more visible activity.
wh: The hard part is feedback. A platform can look successful because the archive is growing and questions are being answered faster, while the underlying sources of quality are weakening. If model-written material enters the archive, later models may train on more machine-made material. If people lean on assistants, they may learn less from direct study. If a gate admits too much weak machine content, archive quality can fall; if it is too strict, useful growth may slow. These forces do not act one at a time. Human inflow, model inflow, query volume, human learning, and model training all push on each other. That is why a static comparison, such as counting how many edits came from humans versus models in one month, misses the central risk. The same policy can lead to different steady states in different domains because PubMed, GitHub with Copilot, and Wikipedia have different growth rates, moderation habits, and learning paths.
naive: A smart beginner might count content volume and average quality separately: more pages, papers, or code snippets means growth, and a moderation score estimates whether the archive is still good. That fails because the danger is not only the current pile. It is the direction of the loop that creates the next pile. A small drop in human contribution can matter if human work is the main source that keeps model training fresh. A small rise in machine additions can matter if those additions later become training material. The beginner's measurement treats people, archives, and models as separate boxes, but the paper's problem is that each box changes the others over time.
ap: The core move is to turn the web knowledge ecosystem into a set of coupled flows. There are inflows of human content and model content into the archive. A gate controls how much model content is admitted. People can improve by studying the archive or by getting help from a language model. The model can improve by training on the corpus or by learning from human feedback. The model then asks what happens when these paths reinforce each other or weaken each other. Instead of declaring one policy good in general, the paper changes levers such as gate strictness, training mode, and human learning pathway, then watches which regime appears: healthy growth, inverted flow where machine additions overtake human inflow, inverted learning where assistance replaces skill building, or oscillations where the system swings rather than settles.
mech: The mechanism starts with five state variables: how large the archive is, how good the archive is, how skilled the model is, how skilled people are in aggregate, and how much query demand exists. At each simulated step, the archive receives two kinds of new material. Human inflow depends on the human side of the system; model inflow depends on the model side and is filtered by an admission gate. The archive's quality then changes according to the quality of what entered and the existing archive. Human skill changes through two pathways: direct study of the archive and assistance from the model. Model skill changes through two training routes: scaling from the corpus and learning from human feedback. Query volume is part of the loop because demand affects use, and use can affect what gets added or learned. Numerical experiments repeatedly update these quantities and look for long-run patterns. The paper then varies platform and policy settings to see where boundaries lie between regimes. PubMed and GitHub with Copilot are used as contrasting domain configurations, and Wikipedia knowledge flow is fit separately for pre-ChatGPT and post-ChatGPT eras to compare whether observed human and model additions match a model-predicted regime.
math: The main mathematical idea is a dynamical system: a way of describing several quantities whose next values depend on their current values and on each other. In everyday terms, it is like tracking water levels in connected tanks, where opening one valve changes not only one tank but the pressure on the rest. Here the tanks are archive size, archive quality, model skill, human skill, and query volume. The valves are human content inflow, model content inflow, gate strictness, archive study, model assistance, corpus-driven training, and feedback-driven training. The model also uses steady-state thinking: if the flows balance, the system settles; if they do not, it can drift, reverse, or oscillate. Numerical experiments mean the equations are run forward under chosen settings rather than solved only by hand. The useful tradeoff is simplicity versus realism. A minimal model cannot capture every platform detail, but it can expose which feedback signs matter: whether machine assistance raises human ability or replaces learning, whether admitted model content improves or dilutes the archive, and whether human feedback keeps the model tied to high-quality human knowledge.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's language-model work because it treats models not as isolated answer machines but as actors inside the data supply chain that future models and people depend on. It also connects to misinformation and trust: quality dilution and model collapse are not just content errors, they are system-level failures where weak material can circulate and become evidence for later decisions. The paper touches recommendation and retrieval indirectly through query volume, because the archive is useful only if people ask for, find, and consume knowledge. It also sits near systems and policy work: the central objects are levers, gates, flows, and resource constraints rather than a single prediction score. Its broader family is human-AI knowledge dynamics, where the recurring problem is how to keep useful human signal alive when automated tools can produce and consume material at high speed.
ww: The model can help because feedback loops often have behavior that is invisible from local inspection. Looking only at one edit, one answer, or one training example cannot reveal whether the long-run loop is healthy. By keeping the main moving quantities separate, the model can show when a change that looks beneficial in one place has a delayed cost elsewhere. For example, easier learning through model assistance can increase short-term productivity, but if it reduces direct archive study, aggregate human skill may weaken. More model additions can grow the archive, but if gate strictness is low and quality is weaker, future training material can become worse. Human feedback can counter that if it anchors model improvement to skilled human judgment. The paper's regime boundaries matter because they turn vague concerns into conditional claims: under these settings, the system settles; under those settings, flow or learning inverts. That is stronger than saying AI content is good or bad in general.
po: The payoff is a way to reason about sustainable web knowledge growth before a platform sees irreversible decay. The model identifies regimes such as healthy growth, inverted flow, inverted learning, and oscillation, and it shows how gate strictness, model training choices, and human learning pathways can move the system across boundaries. The PubMed and GitHub-Copilot configurations illustrate why domains with different moderation norms and growth rates can settle differently. The Wikipedia fit gives empirical grounding: after ChatGPT, the repo data says the paper finds rising model additions with declining human inflow, consistent with one model regime.
limits: The abstract describes a minimal, interpretable model, so its strength is also its limit. It depends on whether archive size, archive quality, model skill, human skill, and query volume can be measured well enough to fit the equations. It assumes the chosen flows capture the important feedback paths and that domain configurations such as PubMed or GitHub-Copilot can be represented by a small set of rates and norms. Numerical regimes are not proof that a specific platform will collapse or grow; they show what follows if the model's assumptions hold. The Wikipedia fit is suggestive, but the abstract does not prove that the model explains every cause of post-ChatGPT contribution change.
